title: Insurance Information Collection

sections.learningObjectives:
- Collect and accurately capture patient insurance and demographic information during registration.
- Distinguish primary and secondary insurance and apply coordination-of-benefits ordering.
- Explain eligibility and benefit verification concepts and follow policy when coverage is unclear.
- Protect the confidentiality of insurance and health information during collection and verification.
- Recognize scope-of-practice boundaries and escalate coverage and billing questions to qualified staff.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Imagine mailing a letter: you need the correct address and stamp or it will not arrive. Collecting insurance information is like getting the right address and stamp so the bill reaches the right company.

### Question 2

An insurance card is like a library card: it has your member number and other details so the right account can be found.

### Question 3

If two people offer to pay for your lunch, you need to know who pays first and who covers the rest. Primary insurance pays first, and secondary covers what is left.

### Question 4

The subscriber is like the person who owns the family phone plan: other family members use it, but the account is in the owner's name.

### Question 5

If you are on a parent's or spouse's plan, the card has their name and number on it. That is the name and number the bill must use.

### Question 6

A group number is like a class number at school: it tells the insurance company which team or plan you belong to.

### Question 7

The back of the card is like the instructions on the back of a box: it tells you where to send things and who to call.

### Question 8

Your name is the key that opens your account. If it is spelled wrong, the key does not fit and the bill bounces back.

### Question 9

A zero and the letter O look alike but are different, like a lowercase 'l' and the number '1'. You must copy each one exactly.

### Question 10

Checking the name and birthday on both cards is like matching two puzzle pieces to be sure they belong together.

### Question 11

Insurance cards are like library cards that get updated: the old one may no longer work, so you check for the newest one each visit.

### Question 12

The guarantor is the grown-up who promises to pay the part of the bill that insurance does not cover.

### Question 13

If someone forgets their library card, the librarian can still look up their account by name. The office tries to find the coverage the same way instead of guessing.

### Question 14

Copying the card is like copying a recipe: every number and letter has to be written exactly right or the result will be wrong.

### Question 15

If a kid is on a parent's insurance, the bill uses the parent's name and number because the parent is the account owner.

### Question 16

Insurance details are like a secret: you only tell people who truly need to know, like the billing team or the insurance company.

### Question 17

Your birthday is a clue that helps the office make sure they have the right person, like a second piece of a name tag.

### Question 18

The assistant is like a messenger: they collect the information and pass the question to the experts who know the exact answer.

### Question 19

The payer is the company or program that writes the check to pay the doctor, like Medicare or a big insurance company.

### Question 20

CMS is the government office that runs Medicare, like the office that runs a big national program.

### Question 21

'Active' is like a gym membership that is still open and working, not cancelled.

### Question 22

A copay is like a small ticket price each time; a deductible is like paying out of your own pocket first until you reach a certain amount, then insurance helps.

### Question 23

You would not announce a friend's secret to a whole room. Insurance details are private, so they are shared quietly, only with people who need to know.

### Question 24

To send a bill you need the account owner's name, account number, and which company to send it to.

### Question 25

If you move, you tell people your new address so mail finds you. The office updates the record so bills and papers go to the right place.

### Question 26

If two friends split the cost of a pizza, one pays first and the second covers what is left. Insurance works the same way with primary and secondary plans.

### Question 27

If both parents have plans, the parent whose birthday comes first in the year has the plan that pays first.

### Question 28

COB is like two friends splitting one bill carefully so they do not both pay for the same slice twice.

### Question 29

Your own work plan is like your own lunchbox: it is the first place to look before borrowing from a friend.

### Question 30

If you have Medicare and a big-company work plan, the work plan usually pays first and Medicare pays second.

### Question 31

Medicare is the main payer and Medicaid helps clean up what is left over, so Medicare goes first.

### Question 32

Medicaid is like the last helper who steps in after everyone else has paid their share.

### Question 33

Eligibility is 'are you allowed in the club?' and benefits are 'what does your membership cover?'

### Question 34

Before the visit, the office calls or checks the insurance company's website to make sure the membership is still turned on.

### Question 35

Checking the oven works before you bake a cake is smarter than finding out after. The office checks coverage before the visit for the same reason.

### Question 36

If the office finds the insurance is turned off, they tell the patient and figure out the next step together instead of pretending everything is fine.

### Question 37

A referral is like a permission slip from your main doctor to go see a special doctor.

### Question 38

An HMO is like a club where your main doctor has to sign a note before you visit a special doctor.

### Question 39

Prior authorization is asking the insurance company for an 'OK' before doing something, so the bill will be covered.

### Question 40

The copay is the small ticket price you pay each time you use your insurance, like a cover charge.

### Question 41

In-network doctors have a special deal with the insurance company, like a restaurant that has a deal with a food delivery app.

### Question 42

Your membership could be turned off between visits, so the office checks each time to be sure it still works.

### Question 43

Writing down who checked, when, and what they found is like keeping a receipt so you can prove what happened later.

### Question 44

You only give the person on the phone the exact pieces they need, like a store clerk who only needs your account number, not your life story.

### Question 45

Assignment of benefits is like telling the insurance company, 'Pay the doctor directly instead of sending me the check.'

### Question 46

If a kid is on the parent's plan, the office notes that the parent is the account owner and the kid is a dependent.

### Question 47

If a page of instructions is torn, you ask for a new copy instead of making up the missing steps.

### Question 48

Money and insurance talk is private, like whispering a secret, so it is done away from other people's ears.

### Question 49

Papers with private information get shredded, like cutting up a secret note before throwing it away.

### Question 50

If you write the wrong account number on a form, the company cannot find you. Accurate entry at the desk stops these mix-ups.

### Question 51

Checking benefits is like checking the menu before ordering to see what is included and what costs extra.

### Question 52

The assistant checks the plan or asks the experts instead of making up an answer about what medicine is covered.

### Question 53

Your member number is like the key to your private health file, so it must be kept safe from strangers.

### Question 54

If two name tags do not match, you ask which is right before writing anything down.

### Question 55

Coinsurance is like splitting a bill by a percentage, such as paying 20 percent while the insurance pays 80 percent.

### Question 56

You re-check the weather each morning, not just once a year, because it changes. Insurance is checked the same way.

### Question 57

A clearinghouse is like a mail sorting center that makes sure each electronic message reaches the right insurance company.

### Question 58

The assistant gathers the facts and passes tricky money and billing questions to the experts, like a messenger.

### Question 59

A waiting period is like a new gym member having to wait a month before using the pool.

### Question 60

Writing the right company name is like putting the right address on an envelope so it arrives at the right mailbox.

### Question 61

When unsure who pays first, the office follows the rules or asks a supervisor, just like checking a rulebook when two people both want to pay.

### Question 62

Electronic health details are locked with a password, and you never share your password, just like you do not share your locker code.

### Question 63

If you have Medicare and are on a spouse's big-company plan, the work plan pays first and Medicare fills in the rest.

### Question 64

A COB form is like a worksheet that lists all your coverages to figure out which one pays first.

### Question 65

If someone gets hurt at work, the work-injury insurance (like a special fund) pays for that injury, not their regular health plan.

### Question 66

An HMO is like a closed club with a main-doctor gatekeeper; a PPO is more like a flexible pass that works at more places.

### Question 67

If the plan says 'get permission first,' the office asks for permission before doing the service, just like asking a parent before a field trip.

### Question 68

If someone changes their name after a wedding, the office updates the records so the bill still matches the insurance company's file.

### Question 69

Leaving a private card in the open is like leaving your diary open on a table where anyone can read it.

### Question 70

Even if a friend says 'tell everyone my secret,' a good friend still keeps it private. The assistant keeps it quiet too.

### Question 71

Routine tasks the assistant can do; tricky money questions go to the experts, like calling a manager when a customer's bill looks wrong.

### Question 72

You have to hand the check to the first person in line before the second person will pay their share.

### Question 73

A pass that only works in emergencies does not work for a regular visit, so the office checks before the appointment.

### Question 74

If a copy of the card is clear, the office can use it and double-check the details, just like using a clear photocopy of a permission slip.

### Question 75

You only open the file you need for your job, not every drawer in the cabinet.

### Question 76

New babies have to be added to the insurance list by a deadline, like signing up for a class before it fills.

### Question 77

Private mail, whether on paper or computer, stays in a locked, secure place, not out in the open.

### Question 78

Being a member of the club does not mean every activity is free; some things still need approval or are not included.

### Question 79

Keep both cards on file, labeled 'first' and 'second,' and send the bill to the second one only after the first one is done.

### Question 80

The effective date is like the day a gym membership actually starts working, not when you first used it.

### Question 81

If someone has no membership card, the office still helps them and figures out how they will pay, instead of turning them away.

### Question 82

An EOB is like a receipt that shows exactly what the insurance paid and what is left for the patient to pay.

### Question 83

The out-of-pocket max is like a safety cap: once you pay that much in a year, the insurance takes over and pays the rest.

### Question 84

Timely filing is like a homework due date: turn the claim in on time or it will not be accepted.

### Question 85

Medicare Advantage is like choosing a private company's plan instead of the government's basic plan, but the company must be approved by Medicare.
